question: Explain how the density of a gas at STP can be used to determine its molar mass and discuss the limitations of the ideal gas law by describing the van der Waals equation.
answer: The density ($\rho$) of a gas at STP is related to its molar mass (M) by M = $\rho \times 22.4$. For example, if a gas has a density of $1.25\ \text{g L}^{-1}$ at STP, then M = $1.25 \times 22.4 = 28\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. The ideal gas law assumes molecules have no volume and exert no intermolecular forces, which is not true for real gases. Van der Waals corrected this with the equation $\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$, where 'a' accounts for intermolecular attraction and 'b' for the volume occupied by the molecules themselves.
anchor: Equal volumes of all gases, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, contain an equal number of molecules. One mole of any gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$ at STP ($0\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$, 1 atm). A gas has a density of $1.25\ \text{g L}^{-1}$ at STP, so $M = \rho\times22.4 = 1.25\times22.4 = 28\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. The deviation arises because two of the postulates are false for a real gas: molecules do attract one another, and they do occupy volume. Van der Waals corrected the ideal gas equation for both: $$\left(P + \frac{an^{2}}{V^{2}}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$
